units.title: Tools of the Trade
units.blurb: Units, significant figures, graphs and the statistics of many launches: how to record a flight so the numbers mean something.

units.title: Pushing Off
units.blurb: Newton's laws, thrust, impulse, the rocket equation and nozzles, all as ideas and numbers, never as building plans.

units.title: Up and Down
units.blurb: Calculus of motion, powered flight, coasting to the top, energy, drag, stability and range.

units.title: How High Did It Go?
units.blurb: Measuring height from the ground with angles: the tangent, the size of the error, and two observers.

units.title: Beyond the Sky
units.blurb: Why Sputnik didn't fall, how fast you must go to leave Earth, and the ellipses of Kepler.

topics.title: Units and Significant Figures
topics.short: Change feet to meters and miles to feet with conversion factors, and keep only as many digits as the measurement deserves.
topics.trouble: Students flip a conversion factor upside down, or copy every calculator digit into the answer.

topics.title: Graphing Flight Data
topics.short: Read a rocket's velocity-time graph: the slope is acceleration, the area is height, and the top of the flight is where the line crosses zero.
topics.trouble: Students think the rocket is highest where the velocity graph is highest, at burnout, instead of where velocity reaches zero.

topics.title: Statistics of Repeated Launches
topics.short: Fly the same rocket again and again: the mean says what to expect, and the range and standard deviation say how much to trust it.
topics.trouble: Students treat one launch as the answer, or confuse the range with the standard deviation.

topics.title: Newton's Three Laws and Thrust
topics.short: A rocket pushes its exhaust down and the exhaust pushes the rocket up. Net force, not thrust alone, sets the acceleration.
topics.trouble: Students divide thrust by mass and forget that weight pulls down the whole time.

topics.title: Thrust-to-Weight and Liftoff
topics.short: A rocket leaves the pad only if its thrust beats its weight. The ratio of the two tells how hard it jumps and how fast it leaves the launch rod.
topics.trouble: Students think any thrust at all will lift a rocket.

topics.title: Impulse, Momentum and Thrust Curves
topics.short: Total impulse is the area under the thrust curve. It equals the change in momentum, and it is what a motor's letter class measures.
topics.trouble: Students multiply peak thrust by burn time instead of finding the area under the whole curve.

topics.title: Mass Flow and the Rocket Equation
topics.short: As a rocket throws mass backward it gets lighter. Adding up those small pushes with calculus gives Tsiolkovsky's equation, $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_0/m_f)$.
topics.trouble: Students use the propellant mass, or the ratio upside down, inside the logarithm.

topics.title: Nozzles in Concept
topics.short: Why a rocket nozzle narrows and then widens: pressure turns into exhaust speed, and faster exhaust means more thrust from the same mass flow.
topics.trouble: Students assume a wider pipe always slows a gas, which is true below the speed of sound but not above it.

topics.title: Calculus of Motion
topics.short: Velocity is the derivative of height, and the change in velocity is the area under the acceleration graph.
topics.trouble: Students evaluate the height function where they need its derivative, or forget the starting value after integrating.

topics.title: Powered Flight to Burnout
topics.short: While the motor burns, the net force gives a steady acceleration (in a simple model). Burnout speed and height follow from the kinematic equations.
topics.trouble: Students use the acceleration from thrust alone, without subtracting gravity.

topics.title: Free Fall and Coasting to Apogee
topics.short: After burnout the rocket is still going up, slowing by 9.8 m/s every second until it stops at apogee.
topics.trouble: Students think the rocket starts falling the moment the motor stops.

topics.title: Energy From Burnout to Apogee
topics.short: Kinetic energy at burnout turns into potential energy on the way up. Comparing the two shows how much energy drag took.
topics.trouble: Students set kinetic energy equal to potential energy measured from the ground instead of from burnout.

topics.title: Drag: A First Look, Then a Numerical Step
topics.short: Air pushes back harder the faster you go, about as the square of speed. With drag there is no neat formula, so we step through the flight a little at a time.
topics.trouble: Students add the drag force in the wrong direction, or forget that it changes as the speed changes.

topics.title: Stability: Center of Mass and Center of Pressure
topics.short: A rocket flies straight when its center of mass is ahead of its center of pressure, so a gust turns it back into the wind like a weather vane.
topics.trouble: Students think the fins should be near the middle, or that a heavier tail makes a rocket steadier.

topics.title: Projectile Range and Launch Angle
topics.short: Tilt the flight and some of the speed carries the rocket sideways. Range depends on the angle, with the longest at 45 degrees in the ideal case.
topics.trouble: Students use the full speed in both the sideways and the up-and-down equations.

topics.title: Altitude by the Tangent
topics.short: Stand a measured distance from the pad, sight the rocket at its highest point, and the tangent of the angle times the baseline gives its height.
topics.trouble: Students use sine instead of tangent, or leave the calculator in radians.

topics.title: How Good Is the Estimate?
topics.short: A one-degree slip in the angle changes the height by an amount that grows fast at steep angles. Choosing the baseline well keeps the error small.
topics.trouble: Students assume the error in height is the same whatever the angle.

topics.title: Triangulating From Two Observers
topics.short: Two people sighting the same rocket from two places can find its height without measuring the distance to the rocket at all.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the near and far observers' angles, or add cotangents when the observers stand on the same side.

topics.title: Why Sputnik Didn't Fall
topics.short: An orbiting satellite is falling all the time, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it.
topics.trouble: Students think there is no gravity in orbit.

topics.title: Escape Velocity
topics.short: Fast enough and an object never comes back: kinetic energy beats the whole gravitational well. Escape speed is $\sqrt{2}$ times circular orbit speed.
topics.trouble: Students measure the distance from the surface instead of from the planet's center.

topics.title: Ellipses and Kepler's Laws
topics.short: Real orbits are ellipses with Earth at one focus. The satellite speeds up near the low point, and the size of the ellipse sets the period.
topics.trouble: Students use altitudes above the ground instead of distances from Earth's center.
